Q: Methods to detect a public IP address in Bash A:

How much public public IP address are you looking for? What if the machine is behind a NAT?

  • curl / wget / netcat (nc) <URL> which contains requester's address: should work most of the time, but may the site may be unreachable from the machine (be it firewall or temporary/permanent unavailability). You'll get the most public IP you can.

  • ifconfig: must run as root, otherwise you'd have to try /sbin/ifconfig or /usr/sbin/ifconfig as well. What if the machine has more NICs? How do you tell what IP address is the right one? What if only IPv6 is used on the machine's LAN? In any case, you'll get the least public IP you can (and possibly a wrong one if more interfaces are configured on the machine - which often is the case these days with omnipresent virtualization using network tap devices and/or).

  • /etc/hostname: does not need to exist, on many systems it is /etc/HOSTNAME, and it does not contain IP address rather it should contain the hostname (usually the FQDN).

The point is, that the ways in which it can fail are numerous and you probably should consider either a) specifying more precisely what systems you are targeting or b) whether you really need to know the IP address at all. Is a solution that seems to work in simple cases worth using when it fails miserably in slightly more complicated setup? If you think you need the IP address, prepare a way to handle failures gracefully in cases where you either don't get the IP address at all or you get a wrong one.

Q: Preference between front-end frameworks? A:

If you want a secondary front-end framework to teach alongside Bootstrap, the top recommendation is Tailwind CSS.

  • Tailwind CSS – modern, widely used, utility-first approach teaches responsive design and component-driven thinking. Great for current job market skills.

Other options to know:

    • Bulma

    • Foundation

    • Materialize

Q: Best algorithm for doing fixed-point euclidean difference? A:

If you have an algorithm that only works for 2D, you can extend it to 3D by doing hypot(hypot(dx, dy), dz).

If you have an algorithm that needs a starting range, you can use max(dx, dy, dz) as your lower bound, and dx + dy + dz as your upper bound. The simplest such algorithm would be to binary search this range to find the square root by seeing which number squared is closest to distance_Squared.

Q: Secrets manager extremely slow in EC2s via awscli and boto3 A:

Extending @LTAcosta 's answer, which correctly identifies the root cause as an IPv6 resolution issue leading to a connection timeout before falling back to IPv4.

Rather than disabling IPv6, I recommend properly configuring it to avoid potential side effects. In my case, the fix was simply enabling outbound IPv6 traffic in the security group associated with my resources. This resolved the 3 minute lag for each secret access attempt, whether via awscli, boto3, or SDKs and it works reliably for both EC2 instances and ECS Fargate tasks (personally tested via boto3).

Notably, it even handles cases where a secret is intentionally inaccessible due to missing permissions (e.g., the timeout doesn't occur; it just fails quickly as expected). If you're using infrastructure as code (e.g. CDK), add these settings to your security group resource:

allow_all_ipv6_outbound = true  # Don't forget this to enable outbound IPv6 (::/0)
allow_all_outbound = true       # For outbound IPv4 (0.0.0.0/0). This should already be enabled in your case.

Be sure to review and tighten these rules as needed for your security posture, but this baseline configuration should eliminate the IPv6-related delays.

A feature request is pending in boto at the time of writing this https://github.com/boto/boto3/issues/3632#issue-1634457296
